newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW -Black watches copper from the sidelines.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -Black watches copper from the sidelines.

text.p: An echo from the Sumitomo scandal rippled through the red metal market Tuesday as prices sparked into life amid talk that the hike was due to Canadian trader Herbert Black covering a short position that was being relentlessly squeezed.

Black, who owns Montreal-based American Iron & Metal scrap company, hit the headlines for his profitable role in shorting the market, helping to push Sumitomo Corp spectacularly into the red last June.
"I have absolutely no position so it's impossible to be squeezed," Black told Reuters Tuesday. "I have been out of the market for some time. I am not long either."

But he would say that, wouldn't he, was the response of some analysts to Black's comments, though the Canadian was adamant about his distance from the copper market in the past two months as he works on several Canadian business projects.
Copper inventories were too low to go short because anyone with deep pockets could take control of them, Black said.
And for those tempted to go long, it was unclear just when the market would lose its current luster.
Earlier Tuesday some brokers were privately voicing concerns about what they see as "games" being played with LME stocks in the U.S. and Asia to push LME into a premium over COMEX in the spot month.
"I would not want to even think of going short until sometime in the end of May or early June," Black said. "The price is reflecting fair value at this given time."
Leaving aside Tuesday's flurry, Black said there was broader concern in the market about declining volumes and open interest on LME and COMEX.
Dwindling turnover has made the risk reward too narrow, and made it difficult to buy or sell large volumes and get out of those positions, Black believed.
People have pulled back from trading because they were no longer able to wager against the price of copper moving up or down, but were betting "against the house".
Punters faced a risky situation because any one of several major trade houses could easily control what little stocks are left while the upside and downside price potential was limited, Black said.
Recently Lehman Brothers pulled out of LME ring dealing, and blue chip J P Morgan scaled down its London base metals trading.
"This is an evolution," Black said, adding he expected more people to leave.
New production will only come on stream measurably in the third and fourth quarter of this year.

"Until then, I don't think there is that much copper about," Black said. "Even if the price of copper is too high right now, and you own it (stocks) all, and you are moving some over and above that, you'll end up walking away with good money. LME won't do anything - they have not up to now so why would they do anything."
People think their chances of succeeding in the copper market are now very limited, and normal hedgers were also afraid to get caught in the current situation, Black said.
